text: Outside of math class, a calculus is the weighing-up of costs, benefits and risks behind a decision — the mental arithmetic someone does when several factors pull against each other. The writer says the evidence points to a straightforward political calculus, more AC for everyone, and then spends the rest of the article explaining why that sum is not simple at all. You will meet the word constantly in phrases like "the political calculus" and "changing the strategic calculus."

Squeamishness is reluctance that comes from distaste rather than from reasoning — being put off by something because it feels wrong or unpleasant. Literally, a squeamish person is easily sickened, by the sight of blood say. Calling the resistance to air-conditioning a stubborn squeamishness is a bit of a jab: it suggests a queasy reaction that has not been fully thought through.

To corrode is literally to eat away at metal, the way rust or acid does; used figuratively it means to weaken something slowly and steadily from within. Nothing is actually rusting here — unreliable electricity gradually eats away at the case for buying an air-conditioner, from the household's side and the power company's side at once. The key idea is slow damage rather than a sudden break.

This is not a row of seats and it does not rhyme with "go" — it rhymes with "cow" and means a noisy quarrel or public argument. It is especially common in British writing, which is why The Economist uses it here for the fight among French politicians over how much air-conditioning is too much.

To be pitted against someone is to be set in direct competition or conflict with them, usually by circumstances rather than by choice. The shoppers here were pitted against each other because there was one portable AC unit left and more than one person who wanted it. You will see the phrase everywhere in writing about contests, wars and lawsuits.

To come to blows is to move from arguing to actually hitting each other — a "blow" here means a punch. The phrase marks the exact moment a dispute turns physical, which is why the detail that two men came to blows in a supermarket does so much work in the opening scene.

Hooligans are rowdy, aggressive troublemakers, especially ones causing havoc in public — the word is most often used in Britain for violent football fans. There is a deliberate joke in calling these people sweat-stained hooligans: they are not thugs at all, just ordinary shoppers who have been reduced to brawling over an air-conditioner.

To heave is to push, pull or lift something heavy with a big physical effort. The crowd heaved against the supermarket doors — leaning and shoving with their combined weight — until the doors gave way. The word carries the sense of straining, not just pushing.

Unrest is widespread public anger that has spilled into action — protests, strikes, riots, blocked roads. It is the standard news word for a situation that is disorderly and tense but has not become an outright uprising. Here, shortages of the energy needed to keep cool have set off unrest in places like Iraq and Sri Lanka.

Allegedly signals that something has been claimed but not proved — journalists use it to report an accusation without stating it as fact. Saying residents allegedly assaulted an electricity-board employee tells you the accusation exists while carefully not asserting that it is true.

Decidedly means definitely or unmistakably — it adds emphasis to whatever adjective follows. Calling the fight over air-conditioning a decidedly modern problem is a way of saying: make no mistake, this could not have happened in any earlier century, since AC barely existed in America before 1960.

Sanitation is the public system for keeping people's surroundings clean and disease-free — sewers, toilets, drainage, rubbish collection. Listing cooling alongside water, energy and sanitation is a strong claim: those three are the classic examples of infrastructure a society simply cannot function without.

Infrastructure is the basic physical machinery a society runs on — roads, pipes, power lines, hospitals. Declaring cooling technologies to be essential infrastructure is a political act, not just a description: once something is called essential, governments are expected to fund it and provide it to everyone, the way they do with clean water.

COP stands for "Conference of the Parties" — the annual United Nations climate summit where nearly every country negotiates over global warming. COP30 was the thirtieth of these, held in Belém, Brazil. Its declarations are not laws, but they set the agenda that governments and development banks then act on.

The Lancet is one of the world's oldest and most respected medical journals, published in Britain since 1823. Naming it matters for the argument: a figure like 489,000 heat deaths a year carries weight precisely because it came from peer-reviewed research there rather than from a campaign group.

In science, modelling means building a mathematical simulation of something too big or too tangled to measure directly, then using it to estimate what you cannot count. Nobody tallied 489,000 heat deaths one by one; researchers estimated them from temperature and mortality data. That is why the article says "according to modelling" — it is a careful signal that the number is a well-founded estimate, not a headcount.

To avert something is to stop it from happening — to head it off before it arrives. Saying AC was averting around 190,000 deaths a year means those people would have died of heat and did not. Averted deaths are always estimates of a thing that did not occur, which is why they come from modelling.

Residential means relating to where people live, as opposed to commercial (shops and offices) or industrial (factories). The distinction is doing real work here: it was residential AC — units in ordinary homes — that cut the risk of dying on a hot day by roughly 75%, not air-conditioned offices and malls.

In this British usage, to reckon is to calculate or judge after weighing the evidence — closer to "estimate" than to the casual American "I reckon so." When researchers reckon that residential AC caused a 75% decline in heat deaths, they mean they worked the figure out, not that they have a hunch.

Rickety means shaky and badly built, liable to collapse — think of a wobbly old wooden chair you would not trust your weight to. Calling electric grids ageing and rickety is a vivid way of saying they are held together with patches and could fail at any moment.

To contend with something is to have to deal with it, usually as an obstacle you would rather not face. Politicians must contend with a public that demands access to AC — meaning that demand is a force they have to manage whether they like it or not. (A different sense of "contend" means to argue a point.)

Outright means openly and completely, with nothing held back. The escalation in "expects, or outright demands" is the whole point of the word: expecting something is quiet, demanding it outright is loud and unmistakable.

Populism is a political style that frames politics as ordinary people versus a self-serving elite; it exists on both the right and the left, which is why the article can describe a populist-right leader and her populist-left rival in the same breath. Note the writer's later jab that Le Pen has "more than populism on her side" — meaning that this time the evidence backs her up, too.

Here "spy" is not espionage — it is the older verb meaning to catch sight of or spot something, especially something others have missed. Populist-right figures spy a clear opportunity: they were the first to notice that public anger about heat could be turned into votes.

The National Rally (Rassemblement National) is France's main hard-right party, led by Marine Le Pen. Knowing that tells you why her call for more air-conditioners in schools and hospitals is notable: it is a populist-right politician campaigning on a public-spending promise usually associated with the left.

Greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane and others — trap heat in the atmosphere, and emissions are the amounts released into it. The figure that cooling produces around 4% of global emissions is the hinge of the argument: air-conditioning protects people from heat while adding, in a small way, to the warming that makes the heat worse.

MAGA stands for "Make America Great Again," Donald Trump's campaign slogan, and is now shorthand for the movement and wing of the Republican Party built around him. The article uses it to explain Ted Cruz's mockery of a request to set thermostats to 78°F — a small culture-war skirmish fought over a thermostat.

A democratic socialist is someone on the political left who wants far more public ownership and a much larger welfare state, but pursues it through elections rather than revolution. The label is included to place New York's mayor on the political map — and to sharpen the contrast when a Texas Republican mocks his energy-saving request.

In geography, temperate describes a mild climate without extremes of heat or cold — the band between the tropics and the polar regions. (In other contexts the same word means self-restrained in behaviour.) Saying Europe is temperate for its latitude sets up the paradox that follows: a mild, wealthy continent that suffers a wildly outsized share of the world's heat deaths.

Latitude is how far north or south of the equator a place sits, measured in degrees. It usually predicts climate — the higher the latitude, the colder — but ocean currents can override it. Europe is warmer than its latitude implies, which is why the article says it is temperate "for its latitude."

A margin is the gap between one thing and the next, so "by a large margin" means not merely first but far ahead of whatever is second. It tells you Europe is not narrowly the worst region for disproportionate heat deaths — it is the worst by a wide gap.

Something is disproportionate when its size is out of line with what you would expect from its share of the whole. Europe holds under 10% of the world's people but suffers about 36% of its heat deaths — roughly four times its share, which is exactly what "kills most disproportionately" is measuring. Learning to compare a share against a base like this is one of the most useful habits in reading statistics.

To attribute an effect to a cause is to assign responsibility for it — in research, to work out how many cases a particular factor accounts for. Heat deaths attributed to Europe are those a statistical model judges to have been caused by heat there. The phrase is a quiet reminder that the number is the output of an analysis, not a body count.

A toll was originally a fee you paid to pass along a road; a death toll is the price paid in lives — the running count of people killed by a disaster, war or epidemic. It is the standard news phrase for a fatality total, and here that annual total has risen by 30% in two decades.

Formidable describes something so large or powerful that it inspires respect, fear, or a sense of being outmatched. Poor countries face formidable budget constraints — not merely tight budgets, but limits big enough to defeat the plan before it starts.

A budget constraint is the economics term for the hard limit set by how much money you have: whatever you buy, the total cannot exceed it, so every purchase rules out another. The article stacks up three costs at once — the units, the electricity, the grid upgrades — which is why the constraint bites on households and governments alike.

A double whammy is two blows landing at once, each making the other worse. Here the two are that the cheapest air-conditioners use the most electricity, and that they are running in the worst-insulated homes — so poor households pay more per unit of cooling twice over.

To gobble something up is to devour it fast and greedily, the way you might eat when starving. Applied to machines and electricity, it is a vivid way of saying the cheapest units consume power at an alarming rate — much more than an efficient model would.

To crank something up is to turn it to a high setting — the image comes from winding a hand crank hard. Cheap air-conditioners are being cranked up in leaky, badly insulated homes: run at full blast, because the cool air keeps escaping.

The breaking point is the moment a thing under strain finally fails — originally an engineering term for the load at which a material snaps. Grids already stretched to breaking point are running so close to their limit that a single hot afternoon can push them over.

Peak demand is the highest amount being used at any single moment, as opposed to the average — and it is the peak, not the average, that a power grid must be built to survive. Air-conditioning is brutal for this because everyone's unit switches on during the same few hot hours: AC is already about a quarter of India's peak demand. It is the same reason school hallways are sized for the four minutes between classes.

A watt measures power — the rate at which energy is used — and a gigawatt is a billion watts, roughly the output of one large power station. So India's cooling demand tripling to 180 gigawatts by 2035 means needing the equivalent of well over a hundred extra power stations running just to keep people cool.

Nothing to do with the robots: a transformer is the electrical device that steps voltage up or down so power can travel long distances on high-voltage lines and then arrive at your house at a usable level. They are the grey drums on utility poles, and when demand spikes they overheat — which is what burned-out transformers means here.

A spot market is where something is bought for immediate delivery at today's price, rather than under a contract agreed in advance. Buying electricity on the spot during a heatwave is like booking a flight the morning you fly: you get it, but at the worst possible price — which is exactly how these utilities lose money whenever demand spikes.

A state-owned company is owned by the government rather than by private shareholders. That ownership is why the article treats these electricity firms as a political problem as much as a business one: their losses land on the public finances, and their decisions about who loses power become decisions a government has to defend.

To sap something is to drain its strength gradually — the word once meant digging away at the foundations of a fortress wall. Losses on emergency power purchases sap the firms' ability to invest: the money is not seized all at once, it bleeds away until nothing is left for repairs.

Sorely means severely or painfully, and it usually attaches to a lack — sorely needed, sorely missed, sorely tempted. Grid improvements that are sorely needed are not merely desirable; their absence is actively hurting people.

A bind is a situation with no good way out, where every option carries a serious cost — the sense of being tied up. The utilities' bind is genuinely tight: cut power and the streets fill with protesters, keep supplying it and the grid collapses anyway.

To hoard is to stockpile something for yourself, especially when it is scarce and others need it. The accusation that governments are hoarding electricity for their own buildings and richer customers is about fairness, not physics: the charge is that a shortage is being shared out unequally.

A subsidy is money a government pays to keep the price of something below its true cost, so people can afford it. Subsidised electricity is a classic example — popular, expensive to sustain, and politically almost impossible to withdraw once people expect it. Note the sting in the article's logic: cheaper electricity means more AC running, which makes the fragile grid fail faster.

A self-reinforcing spiral, or feedback loop, is a process whose result becomes its own cause, so it keeps feeding itself — like a microphone held near a speaker until it screeches. The loop here runs: weak grid, power cuts, costly emergency electricity, deeper debt, no money to fix the grid. Escaping one means breaking a link from outside, which is why the proposed fixes involve development banks and bulk purchasing.

Lee Kuan Yew was Singapore's first prime minister and is regarded as the architect of its transformation from a poor port into one of the world's richest countries. His remark that air-conditioning made development possible in the tropics carries weight because he actually ran a tropical country through that transformation.

A city-state is a sovereign country consisting of a single city and its immediate surroundings — ancient Athens was one, and Singapore and Monaco are modern examples. The term explains itself in context: Lee's city-state is Singapore, a nation of about six million people occupying an island roughly the size of a large city.

The tropics are the hot band of the Earth either side of the equator, between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. Historically almost no rich country was located there, which is the background to Lee Kuan Yew's claim: air-conditioning is what made sustained office work — and so development — practical in that heat.

A host of something means a large number of them. (The word comes from an old term for an army.) Writing that Singapore got rich for a host of other reasons is the writer being careful: he is crediting air-conditioning with helping, while explicitly refusing to claim it did the job alone.

UNICEF is the United Nations agency for children, working on health, nutrition, protection and schooling worldwide. It is the natural source for the figure on over-hot classrooms interrupting the schooling of 130m children in eastern and southern Africa — a reminder that heat costs a country its future workers as well as its present ones.

Heat stress is the physical strain on a body that cannot cool itself fast enough — it makes people slower, clumsier and eventually ill, well before it kills them. That is why it can erase working hours: an outdoor labourer in 45°C heat has to stop, and the International Labour Organisation reckons those lost hours will equal 80m full-time jobs by 2030.

In climate policy, adaptation means reducing the harm from warming that is already coming — sea walls, shaded schools, air-conditioning — as opposed to mitigation, which means cutting emissions to limit the warming itself. Think of a leaking roof: mitigation patches the hole, adaptation puts out buckets. The whole Le Pen–Mélenchon quarrel, and Al Gore's jab about "laziness," is a fight over how much effort should go to each.

To shore something up is to prop it before it collapses — a shore is a support beam braced against a sagging wall. Financing storage and distribution to shore up failing grids means bracing them from outside rather than rebuilding them from scratch.

Bulk-buying is purchasing in huge quantities to get a much lower price per item — the same logic as a family-size box being cheaper per serving. If rich governments bulk-bought efficient air-conditioners, poor countries could get better machines than they could ever negotiate for one at a time.

A patent gives an inventor an exclusive legal right to their invention for a set period, so nobody else may make or sell it without permission; the patent-holder is whoever owns that right. It matters here because the newest, most efficient refrigerants are patented — meaning a handful of firms can decide how expensive hyper-efficient AC stays.

As a verb, to license something is to grant official permission to use it, usually for a fee. Patent-holders licensing refrigerants affordably would mean letting other manufacturers use the patented chemistry cheaply — the difference between a technology existing and a technology being available.

A refrigerant is the fluid inside a cooling machine that carries heat out of the room by evaporating and condensing over and over. Which chemical you use matters twice over: it sets how efficient the unit is, and many refrigerants are themselves potent greenhouse gases if they leak, which is why next-generation ones are worth licensing cheaply.

Passive cooling keeps a building cool without machinery or electricity — insulation, shade, reflective roofs, ventilation, thick walls. It is cheap and permanent, but it can only take the edge off extreme heat, which is the article's complaint: aid programmes favour passive fixes over the air-conditioners poor households actually need.

Not a capital city and not a capital letter: in economics, capital is money available to be invested in building things — factories, grids, machinery. Saying capital remains in scarce supply means the money to finance cooling for poor countries simply is not being put up, a gap the International Finance Corporation sizes at $400bn–800bn.

Emerging markets is the standard finance term for countries partway between poor and rich — growing fast, industrialising, but with less developed financial systems and more risk for investors. India, Brazil and Indonesia are typical examples, and they are exactly where the cooling shortfall is largest.

A shortfall is the gap between what you have and what you need — the amount by which something falls short. The cooling-access shortfall is the distance between the air-conditioning poor countries have now and the amount required to keep people safe, priced here at $400bn–800bn.

A façade is the front, outward-facing wall of a building (the word is French, and in a different sense means a false front someone puts on). European rules restricting the drilling of façades protect the appearance of old buildings — which is why the bestselling air-conditioner is a portable unit that needs no hole in the wall.

A stampede is a panicked mass rush, originally of cattle bolting all at once. Ending on the stampede to buy air-conditioners closes the loop with the opening scene at the Lidl: the writer's point is that the political argument about whether people should have AC has already been settled by people simply going out and buying it.
